_provenance.notes: Alaska salmon ex-vessel prices tell the economic story of the industry: the 1980s-1990s boom ($1.50-2.50/lb sockeye), the catastrophic 1999-2005 price crash driven by Chilean farmed salmon flooding global markets ($0.18-0.38/lb), the slow recovery 2006-2015, and the 2022 record ($2.42/lb sockeye; $10.24/lb Chinook). The price crash of 1999-2005 was the worst economic crisis in Alaska commercial fishing history — permit values fell 60-70%, many boats went bankrupt, and coastal communities suffered. The crash was caused by the global expansion of Chilean and Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon, which priced out wild Alaska product in most restaurant and foodservice markets.

price_crash_narrative.primary_cause: Global expansion of Chilean and Norwegian farmed Atlantic salmon
price_crash_narrative.market_impact: Farmed salmon entered foodservice and retail at $1.50-2.50/lb — the same price point as Alaska wild salmon. As farmed volume grew, prices fell. Restaurant chains (Red Lobster, Olive Garden) switched to farmed product. Alaska lost 60%+ of foodservice market share.

alaska_economic_damage.total_estimated_loss_usd: Over $800M in cumulative lost revenue 1999-2005 vs. 1997 price levels
alaska_economic_damage.bankruptcies: Estimated 800+ fishing boat loan defaults in Alaska
alaska_economic_damage.community_impact: Kodiak, Dutch Harbor, Cordova, Petersburg — all saw 20-35% decline in fishing sector employment

recovery_drivers: ASMI 'Wild Alaska Seafood' marketing campaign — premium restaurant positioning
Japanese market recovery — wild salmon increasingly preferred over farmed
Chilean salmon disease crisis (2007-2010 ISA virus) reduced farmed supply
Whole Foods/premium retail chain growth — wild salmon price premium re-established
Bristol Bay brand development — 'wild sockeye' as premium product
